mcqs.question: What major legal gap was highlighted in connection with the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025?
options: India has no statutory definition of hate speech
India has no provision dealing with untouchability
India has no law on mob lynching guidelines
India has no provision for disqualification for promoting enmity
mcqs.explanation: The highlighted gap was that India has no statutory definition of hate speech. The other options refer to subjects dealt with under other legal provisions or judicial guidelines, not the specific gap identified.

mcqs.question: Under the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, who could face collective liability for hate speech linked to an organisation?
options: Office-bearers of linked organisations
Only Judicial Magistrates First Class
Only members of Parliament
Only members of the Law Commission
mcqs.explanation: The Bill provided for collective liability of office-bearers of linked organisations. Judicial Magistrates First Class are connected with trial of offences, not with this collective-liability provision.

mcqs.question: What power concerning online hateful content was provided under the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025?
options: The State can block or remove hateful content
The State can only issue mob lynching guidelines
The State can only disqualify persons under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
The State can only regulate collective bargaining on digital communication
mcqs.explanation: The Bill empowered the State to block or remove hateful online content. The other options describe different legal or policy subjects and do not state the Bill’s online provision.

mcqs.question:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: BNS Section 353 concerns incitement to offences endangering public order.
Statement B: Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 concerns disqualification for promoting enmity.
options: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
mcqs.explanation: Both statements are correct. BNS Section 353 is associated with incitement to offences endangering public order, while Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 concerns disqualification for promoting enmity.

mcqs.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding existing legal provisions related to hate speech and related offences.

List-I
 a. SC/ST (PoA) Act, 1989
 b. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
 c. IPC 153A conviction rate under NCRB 2020
 d. Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan, 2014

List-II
 i. Asked the Law Commission to define hate speech
 ii. Untouchability
 iii. 20.2%
 iv. Caste-based insults
options: a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i
a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii
a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii
a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv
mcqs.explanation: The correct pairs are a-iv, b-ii, c-iii and d-i. The SC/ST (PoA) Act concerns caste-based insults, the Protection of Civil Rights Act concerns untouchability, the conviction rate was 20.2%, and Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan asked the Law Commission to define hate speech.

mcqs.question:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court’s Tehseen Poonawalla case of 2018 is associated with mob lynching guidelines.
Reason (R): The Bezbaruah Committee of 2014 dealt with racial and regional discrimination.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true. Tehseen Poonawalla is associated with mob lynching guidelines, whereas the Bezbaruah Committee dealt with racial and regional discrimination; the latter does not explain the former.

mcqs.question:
Consider the following statements regarding judicial decisions, committees and reports on hate speech:
1. Shaheen Abdulla (2022) required police to file suo motu FIRs, and this was extended to all States in 2023.
2. Law Commission Report 267 (2017) proposed new Sections 153C and 505A.
3. The Viswanathan Committee (2015) dealt with mob lynching guidelines.
options: 1 and 2 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
mcqs.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Shaheen Abdulla concerned suo motu FIRs, with the direction extended to all States in 2023, while Law Commission Report 267 proposed Sections 153C and 505A; the Viswanathan Committee dealt with identity-based offences, not mob lynching guidelines.

mcqs.question: What was the status of the Hate Speech & Hate Crimes Bill introduced as a Private Member Bill in 2022?
options: It was not passed
It became the first dedicated State law
It was incorporated into the OSH Code, 2020
It was adopted as Law Commission Report 267
mcqs.explanation: The Hate Speech & Hate Crimes Bill introduced as a Private Member Bill in 2022 was not passed. The other options refer to different legislative or report-related developments.

mcqs.question: The Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025 was described as India’s first formal legislative attempt in which area?
options: After-hours digital work
Caste-based insults
Mob lynching guidelines
Untouchability
mcqs.explanation: The Bill was described as India’s first formal legislative attempt concerning after-hours digital work. The other options concern separate areas of hate-speech law and judicial or statutory provisions.

mcqs.question: What was the relationship between the Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025 and the existing labour-law framework?
options: It arose in a context where 29 labour laws had been consolidated into four Labour Codes, while the OSH Code, 2020 was silent on digital labour
It replaced the four Labour Codes with one law on hate speech
It amended Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
It converted mob lynching guidelines into a Labour Code
mcqs.explanation: The Bill was discussed against the backdrop of 29 labour laws being consolidated into four Labour Codes, with the OSH Code, 2020 silent on digital labour. The other options connect the Bill to unrelated legal subjects.

mcqs.question: Which gap was identified in the legal framework surrounding the Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025?
options: There was no definition of digital “work”, and it was not explicitly linked to Article 21
There was no statutory definition of hate speech
There was no provision for caste-based insults
There was no provision for mob lynching guidelines
mcqs.explanation: The identified gap was the absence of a definition of digital “work” and the lack of an explicit link to Article 21. The other options relate to hate-speech legislation or judicial guidelines, not the Right to Disconnect Bill.

mcqs.question: In the European Union context cited in discussions on the Right to Disconnect, what counts as work?
options: On-call time counts as work
Only collective bargaining counts as work
Only work covered by strict hour caps counts as work
Only work defined under the OSH Code, 2020 counts as work
mcqs.explanation: In the cited European Union position, on-call time counts as work, as reflected in the SIMAP, Jaeger and Tyco cases. Collective bargaining and strict hour caps were associated with France and Germany respectively, not the stated EU rule.

mcqs.question: Which pairing correctly describes the approaches of France and Germany to digital communication and working hours?
options: France: collective bargaining on digital communication; Germany: strict hour caps
France: strict hour caps; Germany: collective bargaining on digital communication
France: on-call time counts as work; Germany: mob lynching guidelines
France: digital work has no definition; Germany: hate speech has no statutory definition
mcqs.explanation: France was associated with collective bargaining on digital communication, while Germany was associated with strict hour caps. The first alternative reverses these approaches, and the remaining options concern unrelated subjects.
